```{r setup}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show preliminaries"
library(stLMM)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)

source(file.path(dirname(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)), "utils.R"))

set.seed(1)
```

```{r plot-theme, include=FALSE}
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))
```

## Overview

This vignette introduces directed acyclic graph autoregressive (DAGAR) areal models using `dagar()`. We use Washington counties from `stunitco`, build a county adjacency graph, convert that undirected graph into an ordered directed graph, simulate a Gaussian response from a DAGAR latent effect, fit the model with a few county responses held out, recover the county random effects, and predict the held-out responses.

DAGAR models were developed by @DattaDAGAR2019 as an alternative to common conditional autoregressive (CAR) models for areal spatial smoothing. The starting point is still an areal neighborhood graph, but dependence is represented through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) induced by an ordering of the areal units. This makes the ordering part of the spatial model specification, not just a computational detail.

## Model

For area $i$, the observation model is

$$
y_i = \beta_0 + x_i\beta_1 + w_i + \epsilon_i,\qquad
\epsilon_i \sim N(0,\tau^2).
$$

The DAGAR prior is built from an undirected areal graph and an ordering of its areas. Let $N_\pi(i)$ be the set of directed parents of ordered area $i$ and let $m_i = |N_\pi(i)|$. Under the DAGAR model used by `stLMM`,

$$
w_i \mid \{w_j:j\in N_\pi(i)\}
\sim
N\left(
\frac{\rho}{1 + (m_i - 1)\rho^2}
\sum_{j\in N_\pi(i)}w_j,\,
\sigma^2\frac{1-\rho^2}{1 + (m_i - 1)\rho^2}
\right).
$$

If an ordered area has no parents, the conditional mean is zero and the conditional variance is $\sigma^2$. The parameter $\sigma^2$ controls the marginal scale of the areal process, while $\rho$ controls positive spatial association along the directed parent graph. The implemented model supports $0 \le \rho < 1$; in this example we use a prior bounded away from the endpoints.

The equivalent precision matrix can be written as

$$
\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{dagar}}
=
\sigma^{-2}\mathbf{L}_{\pi}^{\top}\mathbf{F}_{\pi}\mathbf{L}_{\pi},
$$

where $\mathbf{L}_{\pi}$ contains the directed parent coefficients and $\mathbf{F}_{\pi}$ contains the conditional precisions. This is the sparse precision used internally by `stLMM`.

## County graph and ordering

The `stunitco` object contains county polygons for the conterminous United States. Washington has one county that is not connected by polygon boundaries to the rest of the state graph, so we use the same nearest-neighbor bridge rule used in the areal CAR vignette.

```{r wa-graph}
data(stunitco, package = "stLMM")

wa_counties <- stunitco[stunitco$STATECD == 53, ]

g <- car_graph(wa_counties, id = "COUNTYFIPS", island = "nearest", island_k = 4)

g$island_added_edges
```

The undirected graph defines which counties can become DAGAR parent-child pairs. The ordering determines the direction of each eligible edge. For areal graphs built from `sf` polygons, `ordering = "coord"` orders the counties by their point-on-surface coordinates, `ordering = "maxmin"` uses a spatial max-min ordering, `ordering = "hilbert"` uses a Hilbert curve ordering, and `ordering = "random"` samples an ordering.

For user-supplied orderings and a comparison across alternatives, see
[Ordering choices and sensitivity](#ordering-choices-and-sensitivity) near the end
of this article.

The plot below shows the undirected adjacency graph. Bridge edges added for the island county are shown as dashed lines.

```{r undirected-graph, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=4.8}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show graph plotting code"
plot(
  g,
  show_nodes = TRUE,
  show_bridges = TRUE,
  edge_color = "grey45",
  bridge_color = stlmm_color("secondary"),
  node_color = stlmm_color("primary")
)
```

For simulation, we construct the ordered DAGAR precision using `ordering = "coord"`. The helper `dagar_prec()` in `utils.R` follows the same DAGAR precision formula used by the package and stores the ordered graph as an attribute so we can visualize it.

```{r dagar-graph}
sigma_sq <- 1
rho <- 0.7

Q <- dagar_prec(g, sigma_sq = sigma_sq, rho = rho, ordering = "coord")
dg <- attr(Q, "dagar_graph")
```

The directed graph plot shows the parent edges after ordering. Arrows point from parents to children, so each county can depend only on counties earlier in the ordering.

```{r directed-graph, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=4.8}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show directed graph plotting code"
plot(
  dg,
  show_nodes = TRUE,
  edge_color = "grey45",
  node_color = stlmm_color("primary")
)
```

## Data

We construct a county-level covariate from the east-west position of each polygon. This is only for simulation; it gives the fixed-effect part of the model a visible spatial trend. The DAGAR dependence is parameterized through the precision matrix $\mathbf{Q}$. However, in the simulation code below, `rmvnorm()` draws from a covariance matrix, so we compute $\mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{Q}^{-1}$ before drawing the county effects.

```{r simulate-data}
centroid_x <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_centroid(sf::st_geometry(wa_counties)))[, "X"]
centroid_x_mean <- mean(centroid_x)
centroid_x_sd <- stats::sd(centroid_x)

dat <- data.frame(
  area = as.character(wa_counties$COUNTYFIPS),
  county = wa_counties$COUNTYNM,
  x = (centroid_x - centroid_x_mean) / centroid_x_sd
)

beta <- c(0.5, -1)
tau_sq <- 0.1

Sigma <- solve(Q)
w <- rmvnorm(mean = rep(0, nrow(Q)), Sigma = Sigma)
names(w) <- rownames(Q)

dat$w_true <- w[dat$area]

mu <- beta[1] + beta[2] * dat$x + dat$w_true
epsilon <- rnorm(nrow(dat), sd = sqrt(tau_sq))
dat$y_full <- mu + epsilon

holdout_id <- sample(seq_len(nrow(dat)), 6)
dat$sample <- "training"
dat$sample[holdout_id] <- "holdout"

dat$y <- dat$y_full
dat$y[holdout_id] <- NA
```

The mapped response values show the east-west covariate trend plus county-level DAGAR variation. The black outlines mark counties held out from the likelihood.

```{r wa-response-map, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=3.8}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show plotting code"
wa_plot <- wa_counties
wa_plot$area <- as.character(wa_plot$COUNTYFIPS)
wa_plot$y_full <- dat$y_full[match(wa_plot$area, dat$area)]
wa_plot$sample <- dat$sample[match(wa_plot$area, dat$area)]

ggplot(wa_plot) +
  geom_sf(
    aes(fill = y_full),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.15
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = wa_plot[wa_plot$sample == "holdout", ],
    fill = NA,
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = stlmm_palette()) +
  labs(fill = "response")
```

## Fit

Rows with `y = NA` are included in the fitting data so that the fitted graph still contains the held-out counties. They do not contribute to the likelihood, but they remain available for recovery and prediction because their county IDs are part of the DAGAR support.

The residual and process variances use half-$t$ priors on their corresponding standard deviations. The DAGAR association parameter `rho` uses a bounded uniform prior over positive spatial association values.

We use four chains and inspect the post-burn summaries before comparing orderings.
The diagnostics in `summary()` are provided by coda [@PlummerEtAl2006Coda].

```{r fit-dagar}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr digest::digest(list(dat, g, packageVersion("stLMM")))
n_samples <- 12000
burn <- 4000
fit <- stLMM(
  y ~ x + dagar(area, graph = g, ordering = "coord"),
  data = dat,
  priors = list(
    resid = list(tau_sq = half_t(df = 3, scale = 0.5)),
    dagar_1 = list(
      sigma_sq = half_t(df = 3, scale = 1),
      rho = uniform(0.05, 0.95)
    )
  ),
  n_samples = n_samples, chains = 4, chain_control = list(seed = 201),
  n_omp_threads = 1, verbose = FALSE
)

summary(fit, burn = burn)
```

## Recover

Like other structured process terms, DAGAR effects are integrated out during fitting. Calling `recover()` draws the county-level DAGAR effects conditional on the posterior parameter samples.

```{r recover-dagar}
set.seed(301)
rec <- recover(fit, sub_sample = list(start = burn + 1, thin = 20))

rec
```

The recovered `dagar_1` columns are returned in the original graph support order. As in the CAR and NNGP vignettes, the data identify the combined areal intercept, $\beta_0 + w_i$, more directly than the split between the global intercept and the average level of one realized areal process. For this diagnostic, we therefore compare $\beta_0 + w_i$ rather than $w_i$ alone.

```{r recovery-plot, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=4.8}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show plotting code"
rec_draws <- as_samples(rec, include_w = TRUE, metadata = FALSE)
w_cols <- paste0("w_dagar_1_", seq_along(g$ids))
w_hat <- colMeans(rec_draws[, w_cols, drop = FALSE])
names(w_hat) <- g$ids
beta_0_hat <- mean(rec_draws[["(Intercept)"]])

recovery_dat <- data.frame(
  truth = beta[1] + dat$w_true,
  estimate = beta_0_hat + w_hat[dat$area],
  sample = dat$sample
)
recovery_lim <- range(recovery_dat$truth, recovery_dat$estimate)

ggplot(recovery_dat, aes(truth, estimate)) +
  geom_point(
    aes(shape = sample),
    color = stlmm_color("primary"),
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    color = stlmm_color("secondary"),
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  coord_equal(
    xlim = recovery_lim,
    ylim = recovery_lim
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "true areal intercept",
    y = "posterior mean estimate",
    shape = NULL
  )
```

## Predict

DAGAR prediction uses areas that already belong to the fitted graph. Here the held-out counties were included in the original data with `y = NA`, so they can be predicted after recovery.

```{r predict-holdout}
set.seed(302)
holdout_new <- dat[holdout_id, c("area", "x")]

pred <- predict(
  rec,
  newdata = holdout_new,
  y_samples = TRUE
)

summary(pred)
```

The `predict()` call returns posterior draws of the conditional mean $\mu$ and, because `y_samples = TRUE`, posterior predictive response draws. `as_samples()` combines the chains for summarization and can retain chain identifiers for diagnostics.

```{r prediction-plot, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=4.8}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show plotting code"
pred_y <- as_samples(pred, sample = "y", metadata = FALSE)
pred_dat <- data.frame(
  y = dat$y_full[holdout_id],
  y_hat = colMeans(pred_y)
)
pred_lim <- range(pred_dat$y, pred_dat$y_hat)

ggplot(pred_dat, aes(y, y_hat)) +
  geom_point(
    color = stlmm_color("primary"),
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    color = stlmm_color("secondary"),
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  coord_equal(
    xlim = pred_lim,
    ylim = pred_lim
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "held-out response",
    y = "posterior predictive mean"
  )
```

## Extensions

The space-time DAGAR term replaces the CAR spatial component in `car_time()` with a DAGAR spatial component. The time component and data layout follow the same rules as the space-time CAR vignettes. The example below shows the syntax for an areal response indexed by area and time.

```{r dagar-time-syntax, eval=FALSE}
fit_dagar_time <- stLMM(
  y ~ x + dagar_time(area, year, graph = g, ordering = "coord"),
  data = dat,
  priors = list(
    resid = list(tau_sq = half_t(df = 3, scale = 0.5)),
    dagar_time_1 = list(
      sigma_sq = half_t(df = 3, scale = 1),
      rho = uniform(0.05, 0.95),
      phi = uniform(0.05, 0.95)
    )
  )
)
```

Use `time_model = "exp"` when the fitted time support is numeric and temporal association should depend on actual time gaps.

```{r dagar-time-exp-syntax, eval=FALSE}
fit_dagar_time_exp <- stLMM(
  y ~ x + dagar_time(area, decimal_year, graph = g,
                    ordering = "coord", time_model = "exp"),
  data = dat,
  priors = list(
    resid = list(tau_sq = half_t(df = 3, scale = 0.5)),
    dagar_time_1 = list(
      sigma_sq = half_t(df = 3, scale = 1),
      rho = uniform(0.05, 0.95),
      lambda = log_normal(meanlog = 0, sdlog = 1)
    )
  )
)
```

Point observations can also be linked to an areal DAGAR or DAGAR-time support. In that case, each point-level row carries the associated area ID, and multiple point observations can share the same areal latent effect. If you want a random effect or prediction for an area, time, or area-time cell with no observed point rows, include a row with `y = NA` and the associated area, time, and covariate values.

## Ordering choices and sensitivity {#ordering-choices-and-sensitivity}

This optional section examines the choice of spatial ordering. We keep the
simulated data, county graph, covariate, priors, and six held-out counties fixed,
and compare parameters and county means across orderings.

### What changes with ordering?

Changing the ordering changes which adjacent counties are parents, and therefore
changes the DAGAR prior. This differs from `cholmod_control`, which reorders the
same precision matrix for sparse factorization without changing the model.

@DattaDAGAR2019 compare four diagonal sweeps across a map and report similar
latent-effect errors and inference for $\rho$ in their sensitivity experiment
(Section 3.2). Their theoretical variance and neighbor-correlation results apply
to particular tree and grid orderings (Sections 2.3–2.4); they do not establish
invariance under arbitrary orderings on irregular graphs. They also construct an
order-free model by averaging precision matrices. That is a distinct prior,
not an average of fitted predictions, and is not implemented by `dagar()`.

@OrdonezEtAl2026Innovations retain a spatial ordering in their space-time
innovation representation and refer to Datta et al.'s sensitivity findings
(Section 2.3, following equation 13). Thus the ordering question also applies
to space-time DAGAR models. Their innovation representation is discussed in the
[technical article](a12-modeling-software-details.html).

Max-min ordering has a different motivation in Vecchia GP approximations
[@Guinness2018Vecchia]. Those approximation results do not establish an optimal
DAGAR ordering. Here we focus on diagonal sweeps and the package default.

### Default and user-supplied orderings

The default is `ordering = "coord"`. For an `sf` graph, it orders polygon
point-on-surface coordinates lexicographically: first by the first coordinate,
then by the second to break ties. For an adjacency-matrix graph without geometry,
it preserves the supplied graph-node order. This is a reproducible starting point,
not a universally optimal statistical choice.

Both `dagar()` and `dagar_time()` also accept a numeric permutation of `1:g$n`.
The numbers identify nodes in the order of `g$ids`, not county identifiers or
observation-row indices. There is one index per graph node, including counties
without responses. The same spatial ordering is used across times in
`dagar_time()`.

For this Washington example, use projected coordinates in meters (EPSG:5070).
The four sweeps below are geographic analogs of the diagonal orderings studied
by Datta et al. Point-on-surface coordinates follow the graph's node order.
The default lexicographic ordering is kept as a fifth reference fit.

```{r diagonal-orderings}
coords <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_point_on_surface(
  sf::st_transform(g$geometry, 5070)
))
east <- coords[, "X"]
north <- coords[, "Y"]

# Start in one corner and sweep approximately toward the opposite corner.
sw_ne <- order(east + north, east, north)
nw_se <- order(east - north, east, north)
orders <- list(
  Default = "coord",
  "SW to NE" = sw_ne,
  "NE to SW" = rev(sw_ne),
  "NW to SE" = nw_se,
  "SE to NW" = rev(nw_se)
)
```

The named options `"maxmin"`, `"hilbert"`, and `"random"` remain available.
Max-min and Hilbert require an `sf` graph; random ordering should be generated
once with a recorded seed and reused across chains. An explicit permutation can
also encode an application-motivated order. Edge directions alone do not imply
causal relationships.

### Fit the same model under each ordering

We reuse the default fit above and fit four alternatives. Each has four chains
of `r format(n_samples, big.mark = ",")` returned iterations, discards
`r format(burn, big.mark = ",")` per chain, and uses every remaining parameter
draw for diagnostics. Only recovery of county means is thinned. These data were
generated under the default ordering; the exercise demonstrates sensitivity for
one dataset rather than ranking the orderings or estimating repeated-sample
performance.

```{r ordering-diagonal-fits}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: fit-dagar
#| cache.extra: !expr digest::digest(list(dat, g, orders, n_samples, packageVersion("stLMM")))
fit_ordering <- function(ordering, seed) {
  stLMM(
    y ~ x + dagar(area, graph = g, ordering = ordering),
    data = dat,
    priors = list(
      resid = list(tau_sq = half_t(df = 3, scale = 0.5)),
      dagar_1 = list(
        sigma_sq = half_t(df = 3, scale = 1),
        rho = uniform(0.05, 0.95)
      )
    ),
    n_samples = n_samples, chains = 4, chain_control = list(seed = seed),
    n_omp_threads = 1, verbose = FALSE
  )
}

ordering_fits <- list(Default = fit)
for (i in 2:length(orders)) {
  ordering_fits[[names(orders)[i]]] <- fit_ordering(orders[[i]], seed = 202 + i)
}
```

### Compare parameters

The intervals below show how regression and covariance parameter estimates
change with ordering. Process scale and $\rho$ describe the specified DAGAR
prior; their relationship to marginal variances and correlations can also change
with the ordering on an irregular graph.

```{r ordering-parameters}
#| code-fold: true
ordering_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ordering_fits), function(ordering) {
  s <- summary(ordering_fits[[ordering]], burn = burn)
  data.frame(ordering, parameter = rownames(s$parameters),
             mean = s$parameters[, "mean"], lower = s$parameters[, "q2.5"],
             upper = s$parameters[, "q97.5"], rhat = s$diagnostics$rhat,
             ESS = s$diagnostics$effective_size, row.names = NULL)
}))
ordering_table$ordering <- factor(ordering_table$ordering, levels = names(orders))
parameter_order <- c("(Intercept)", "x", "dagar_1_sigma_sq", "tau_sq", "dagar_1_rho")
ordering_table$parameter <- factor(ordering_table$parameter, levels = parameter_order)

ordering_colors <- c(Default = "#263E4E", "SW to NE" = "#236B90",
                     "NE to SW" = "#408A7F", "NW to SE" = "#779D48",
                     "SE to NW" = "#7E6F9E")
parameter_labels <- c("(Intercept)" = "Intercept", x = "Covariate coefficient",
                      tau_sq = "Residual variance", dagar_1_sigma_sq = "Process scale",
                      dagar_1_rho = "Spatial association")
```

```{r ordering-parameter-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.8}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "Posterior means and 95% credible intervals for the same parameters under five spatial orderings. Scales differ across parameters."
ggplot(ordering_table, aes(mean, ordering, color = ordering)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = ordering), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ parameter, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3,
             labeller = as_labeller(parameter_labels)) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(names(orders))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = ordering_colors) +
  labs(x = "Parameter: posterior mean and 95% credible interval", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The covariate's 95% interval remains below zero for every ordering, but its
estimated magnitude changes. Process-scale and association estimates also shift;
their intervals show the uncertainty remaining in this small dataset.

The largest parameter R-hat is `r round(max(ordering_table$rhat), 4)` and the
smallest ESS is `r round(min(ordering_table$ESS))`, using `summary()` and coda
[@PlummerEtAl2006Coda]. Inspect mixing before interpreting differences across
fits. Diagnostics describe these chains, separately from sensitivity to the
assumed spatial model.

<details>
<summary>Parameter estimates, ESS, R-hat, and chain traces</summary>

```{r ordering-summary, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(ordering_table, digits = c(0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 4, 0))
```

```{r ordering-traces, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "Post-burn parameter chains for each ordering. Traces display every twentieth draw; numerical diagnostics use every post-burn parameter draw."
trace_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ordering_fits), function(ordering) {
  draws <- as_samples(ordering_fits[[ordering]], burn = burn, thin = 20)
  parameters <- setdiff(names(draws), c(".chain", ".iteration"))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(parameters, function(parameter) {
    data.frame(ordering, parameter, iteration = draws$.iteration,
               chain = factor(draws$.chain), value = draws[[parameter]])
  }))
}))
trace_data$ordering <- factor(trace_data$ordering, levels = names(orders))
trace_data$parameter <- factor(trace_data$parameter, levels = parameter_order)
ggplot(trace_data, aes(iteration, value, color = chain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.65) +
  facet_grid(parameter ~ ordering, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(parameter = as_labeller(parameter_labels))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = stlmm_discrete_colors(4)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(burn, (burn + n_samples) / 2, n_samples),
                     labels = scales::label_number(scale = 0.001, suffix = "k")) +
  labs(x = "MCMC iteration", y = NULL, color = "Chain") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

</details>

### Compare county means

For every county, compare the latent mean $\mu_a=\beta_0+x_a\beta_1+w_a$.
These are mean responses, including the covariate contribution. We do not add
residual noise here: the comparison is intended to reveal changes in estimated
county means that wider response-prediction intervals could obscure. All fits
use the same 33 observed counties and retain the same six held-out counties.

```{r ordering-area-means}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: ordering-diagonal-fits
#| cache.extra: !expr digest::digest(list(dat, mu, burn, names(orders), packageVersion("stLMM")))
set.seed(303)
area_estimates <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ordering_fits), function(ordering) {
  recovered <- recover(ordering_fits[[ordering]],
                       sub_sample = list(start = burn + 1, thin = 20))
  predicted <- predict(recovered, newdata = dat[, c("area", "x")], y_samples = FALSE)
  draws <- as.matrix(as_samples(predicted, sample = "mu", metadata = FALSE))
  data.frame(ordering, area = dat$area, county = dat$county,
             sample = ifelse(is.na(dat$y), "Held out", "Observed"), truth = mu,
             mean = colMeans(draws), lower = apply(draws, 2, quantile, 0.025),
             upper = apply(draws, 2, quantile, 0.975), row.names = NULL)
}))
area_estimates$ordering <- factor(area_estimates$ordering, levels = names(orders))
default_mean <- setNames(subset(area_estimates, ordering == "Default")$mean, dat$area)
area_estimates$default_mean <- default_mean[area_estimates$area]
```

```{r ordering-area-scatter, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "Posterior mean county estimates under each diagonal ordering versus the default. Each panel contains the same 39 counties; triangles identify the six held out from fitting. Axes are shared and the dashed line marks agreement."
comparison <- subset(area_estimates, ordering != "Default")
area_limits <- range(comparison$mean, comparison$default_mean)
ggplot(comparison, aes(default_mean, mean, color = ordering, shape = sample)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = 2, color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2.3, alpha = 0.85) +
  facet_wrap(~ ordering, ncol = 2) +
  coord_equal(xlim = area_limits, ylim = area_limits) +
  scale_color_manual(values = ordering_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Observed = 16, "Held out" = 17)) +
  labs(x = "Default ordering: posterior mean county response",
       y = "Alternative ordering: posterior mean county response", shape = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The following plot adds uncertainty for the six held-out counties. Dashed lines
show their generating latent means, not their noisy held-out responses.

```{r ordering-heldout-intervals, fig.width=9, fig.height=6}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "Posterior means and 95% credible intervals for the latent means of the six held-out counties. Dashed vertical lines identify the generating latent means."
heldout <- subset(area_estimates, sample == "Held out")
ggplot(heldout, aes(mean, ordering, color = ordering)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = truth), linetype = 2, color = "grey60") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = ordering), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ county, ncol = 3) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(names(orders))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = ordering_colors, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "County latent mean: posterior mean and 95% credible interval", y = NULL)
```

<details>
<summary>Estimates and intervals for every county</summary>

```{r ordering-area-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(area_estimates[, c("county", "sample", "ordering", "mean", "lower", "upper")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

</details>

The largest absolute shift in a county's posterior mean from the default is
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(area_estimates$mean - area_estimates$default_mean)[area_estimates$sample == "Observed"]))`
among observed counties and
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(area_estimates$mean - area_estimates$default_mean)[area_estimates$sample == "Held out"]))`
among held-out counties, in response units. The held-out intervals overlap across
orderings, but their centers and widths differ. This illustrates why checking
area estimates can be informative even when a regression conclusion is unchanged.
It does not establish a generally preferable ordering.

### Practical guidance

Use a recorded, reproducible ordering and check a few plausible alternatives
while keeping the remaining model specification fixed. Compare parameters and
the area means or aggregates that matter for the application, relative to their
posterior uncertainty. Similar answers in this example would not establish
insensitivity for another graph or dataset. If substantive conclusions change,
report that sensitivity and revisit the spatial assumptions. The package
provides general chain diagnostics and prediction tools, but no automatic
ordering-sensitivity score or statistically optimal ordering selector.

## What this example illustrates

The `dagar()` term is for areal data where the latent process is indexed by graph nodes and the graph is converted into an ordered directed parent graph. Prediction is for existing areas in the fitted graph, including areas whose responses were held out with `NA`. The main DAGAR-specific choices are the areal graph and the ordering used to orient that graph.
